title: Europe heatwave energy crisis — climate costs masked by war premium — 2026-05-28
narrative: On May 28, Portugal broke its hottest May day on record. French students took exams in what were described as "baking schools." Italy issued red alerts. Europe is sweltering under a heatwave that is breaking records — in May, not July or August. Simultaneously, UK energy regulator announced a £221/year price cap increase, attributing the rise to "the impact of the Iran war." The climate crisis is producing measurable physical records while energy policy uses geopolitical conflict as cover for price increases. The connection is structural: Europe's failure to decarbonize its energy grid means every geopolitical shock — and every climate extreme — translates directly into household bills. The war premium masks the climate premium.
telemetry: Portugal: hottest May day on record (May 28)
France: schools described as "baking" — exams conducted in extreme heat
UK energy price cap: £221/year increase, attributed to "Iran war impact"
Structural context: Europe's energy transition has not insulated households from fossil fuel price shocks
Open questions: what portion of the £221 increase is actually attributable to Iran war vs. pre-existing gas market dynamics? How much of Europe's power grid still depends on gas-fired generation?
analysis: The Iran war provides convenient cover for energy price increases that climate-driven demand spikes and infrastructure failures would necessitate regardless. Separate the war premium from the climate premium — what portion of the £221 is actually Iran-related versus structural gas market dynamics? Track the correlation between European temperature records and energy price spikes over the past five years. The elite narrative blames geopolitics; the thermometers tell a different story.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: The planet is breaking temperature records while governments blame war for energy bills they failed to decarbonize against — and the bill comes due either way.
